title: The bent made whole
hookLine: bend and be straight, empty and be full (Tao Te Ching 22)

cards: A couch is stuck in a doorway. One person is in the hall, shoving. The other is inside the room, pulling.
The couch doesn't move, and both of them are getting louder. Then a neighbor wanders past, looks for a second, and says, tilt it. Stand it on its end, turn it a little.
The couch slides through as if the doorway had grown. Nobody got stronger. Somebody gave up the straight line.
Chapter twenty-two of the Tao Te Ching is built on that moment, when bending is what gets the thing through.

teach.b: First, bent, then whole. The chapter opens with a run of reversals. In Legge's translation: "The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full; the worn out, new."
Each pair goes against common sense. We expect the bent thing to break. The chapter says the bent thing is the one that stays whole.
Second, empty, then full. A cup that's already full can't receive; only an empty one can be filled. What is worn out makes room for what is new.
Wanting follows the same pattern: whoever wants little, it says, gets it, and whoever wants a lot gets lost.
Third, the sage doesn't push. Then the chapter turns to a person. The sage doesn't put himself on display, and so he shines.
He doesn't insist he's right, and so he stands out. He doesn't boast, and so his work counts. He isn't proud of himself, and so he lasts.
Because the sage doesn't contend with anyone, the chapter says, no one in the world can contend with him. There's nothing to push against.
It closes by asking whether the old saying about the bent being made whole was just empty words. Its answer: no. Becoming whole really comes this way.
Yielding here isn't losing. It's how the couch gets through the door.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching treat chapter twenty-two as a habit for daily life: giving way on small disagreements rather than pressing to win them.

games.q: what does “yield and be whole” mean?
o: giving up every belief to keep the peace
losing on purpose so others feel stronger
bending on small things, which keeps you whole

p: no one can contend with him

s: chapter twenty-two says yielding is a kind of losing
it says the bent is made whole, and the old saying about it is not empty words.
in chapter twenty-two, whoever wants little gets it
and whoever wants a lot gets lost.
the sage in this chapter wins by putting himself on display
he doesn't display himself, and so he shines; he doesn't boast, and so his work counts.

games.q: you're in a standoff that won't move, and you're the sage of chapter twenty-two. what do you do?
o: push harder until the other side gives.
walk off and leave it stuck.
games.why: the sage doesn't contend, and so no one in the world can contend with him. there's nothing left to push against.

practice: Bring to mind one small standoff: where the dishes go, which route to take, a comment you've been waiting to correct. Picture yourself saying fine, your way, and meaning it, and notice what happens in your shoulders.
If it feels like losing, stay with it a moment longer.

wordCard.voice: Yield and be whole. Chapter twenty-two's run of reversals: the bent made whole, the empty filled, and the one who doesn't contend, whom no one can contend with. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, qū zé quán: bent, then whole. The opening words of Tao Te Ching 22.

carryVoice: Your line: the bent is made whole. The one who doesn't contend leaves nothing to push against. I'll be here tomorrow.
